#CompletelyUnexpectedTrueIdentity

by Mother of Pearl (notnacre)

Summary

Jungkook doesn't see any problem with roleplaying whatever kind of character he wants, including a princess. Nobody on the internet is ever who they say they are.

Namjoon knows his new roleplay partner Jungsoon isn't really a runaway princess. That's just a game, but it gets real when he starts to fall for her. It doesn't matter that they've never met irl. His gut tells him he knows everything he needs to about the real girl behind the character.

Chapter 1

👸🏻

Just to see, he decides. He doesn’t have to do anything.

He logs into his new account. There’s no reason to feel nervous or guilty. There’s nothing wrong about what he’s doing. It’s a little out of the ordinary for him, yes, but lots of people do it. That was clear as soon as he scrolled through his first search results last week. It’s just to see. And nobody will know who he is, so what’s the worst that could happen? He forcefully puts aside the feeling that even thinking that question begs a thunderbolt of karmic retribution.

He requests to join the group, and then he waits. And nothing happens. He rereads the profile he put together yesterday. Debates changing a line. Tries it. Puts it back.

The request is still pending. It might be a sign. Yeah, definitely. Everything is fated; that’s what he believes. He gave it a shot, it didn’t work out, and that’s got to mean something. It was a dumb idea anyway. It was just a lark, and he probably isn’t cut out for this kind of thing. He’ll stick with dating sims. He’ll just—

A notification pops up. He’s in.

No expectations, he reminds himself. It’s a big group. Hundreds of members already, and it seems like most of them have been here for a while. He clicks a few profiles, and his feeling that this is alien territory, a place he shouldn’t trespass on, stays with him. Most of the interactions are conducted in private, he knows from the background reading he’s done over the last week. What’s on the profiles and in the feed is for public consumption and doesn’t really tell him much about how this works once you meet someone and make whatever agreement you make. Take your relationship into DMs and then…see if you hit it off. The idea gives him a little thrill of anticipation.

But he doesn’t find anyone who looks promising. Most of them seem to have a set group they regularly interact with, and their posts mostly look like continuations of ongoing conversations that he’d feel awkward barging in on. He drops a couple likes and one or two replies to the ones that seem the least like inside jokes or long-running interactions. The sites he read all said you have to interact a lot at first if you have any hope of this going anywhere, but he doesn’t see any profiles that look like a good match for his. It already feels like wasted effort, and he can’t shake the notion in the back of his mind that even if someone wants to talk to him, it will be so awkward that it will die before it really gets started.

That’s enough for the first day, he decides. He’ll take it at his own pace. And this isn’t the only group he plans to try. Maybe tomorrow he’ll check out another one. He closes the window, but as it’s minimizing into oblivion, he thinks—he might be wrong, but he thinks—was that a notification? No, it was probably nothing. Just a like on one of the throwaway comments he left, probably. But he opens the window again to check. Now it’s two notifications. And before he can even click to see what they are, a third. And a fourth. He clicks.

One like—his pinned profile—and three direct messages from @naegeumwiSC.

He isn’t sure what to do. If he opens the messages, the sender will see that he’s online, and then he’ll have to answer or else snub the person. Maybe he should close the window and come back to it tomorrow. He wasn’t expecting to have to talk to anyone so soon. He thought he’d have a chance to practice with some public messages before moving to a private chat.

On the other hand, the sites he studied to prepare said it can take time and effort before you establish yourself enough in the group to have anyone show an interest in chatting one on one with you, and he isn’t an especially patient person. In fact, the thought of spending weeks replying to other users’ dull public posts in order to build a network of contacts before he gets any action was almost enough to make him scrap the whole idea. It sounded too much like schoolwork. So maybe it would be foolish to pass up this opportunity to skip the small talk and get directly to the reason he’d wanted to try this in the first place.

But also—Naegeumwi. He’s watched enough historical dramas to know they were royal guards. He’s been on the site for less than an hour and already there’s someone—not just anyone, but a royal guard!—who wants to get to know him better? Get to know his character, not him; he has to remember that. But so soon. This isn’t a coincidence. He runs through his character’s bio in his head. Got it. He’s ready. He clicks.

The truth is, Jungkook doesn’t consider himself much of a storyteller. And maybe he didn’t think through this whole plan enough because when he imagined what it would be like, he envisioned it more as a live-action RPG where the world already exists and he just moves around in it and reacts to whatever’s going on. And maybe it was naive of him—it’s called roleplay, after all—but he didn’t expect there to be quite so much acting involved. Maybe if he sticks with it, he could get the hang of the acting thing. Maybe this was just a case of first-time nerves and he’ll warm up to it.

That guy Chongji was really, really into it, though, and it was kind of overwhelming. Watching the messages pop up put him under a lot more pressure than he was ready for. And the guy seemed really formal, kind of stiff— and not in a good way, he mentally adds and snickers to himself. Jungkook can’t shake the impression that the real person behind Chongji is a pervy old man trying to find a young girl to take out his midlife sexual frustration on. Though looking back through the chat, he doesn’t see any major red flags. Yet.

He opens the guy’s profile again. Seol Chong, a royal guard. Age 27—yeah, right. The profile pic the guy has chosen is a handsome warrior in jeonbok, holding a sword. He looks like someone Jungsoon would trust. He looks strong and dependable. Jungkook could just— He could try to ignore whoever the real person is behind the character. That’s what you agree to when you do this, right? That’s what he’s expecting people who meet him this way to do. They won’t be meeting him at all. They’ll only know Jungsoon, and that’s what he’d have to do if he decided to continue. He’d have to put out of his mind any ideas about whoever is behind the character, pretend they don’t exist, and just be Jungsoon talking to Chongji.

It’s worth a try. He’ll give it a shot. Maybe with this Chongji guy, or maybe he’ll meet someone else. It’s only his first day and he’s never been a quitter. And if he gives Chongji a fair try and it still doesn’t work out, he can try some other group, or maybe he’ll forget the whole thing, close his account and stick to gaming, even if it has started to feel sort of dull these days.

With that decided, he shuts his laptop. It’s already starting to get dark outside. He lost track of time again. That happens a lot lately since he spends so much time alone. But the boss is coming tomorrow. It will be nice to have someone else around. He already knows everything is ready for inspection, but it wouldn’t hurt to check one more time. He slips on his shoes and goes out to start his evening chores.

His first mistake was letting his guard down. It seemed safe enough. Just a normal (if extravagant) weeknight dinner with friends. Now he can see that it was a trap. He said yes to a glass of wine, which in retrospect seems calculated to weaken his defenses. Because no sooner is the main course served than the real purpose of the invitation becomes apparent.

“Oh, tell him,” Jimin says, backhanding Seokjin lightly across the chest, “about the thing.” Ignoring his own plate of sad-looking vegetables, Jimin waylays a bite of steak on its way to Seokjin’s mouth and reroutes it to his own.

“What thing?” Namjoon can tell from the set of Seokjin’s smile that he and Jimin had argued about this and Jimin had won. As Jimin does.

Jimin gestures for Seokjin to talk, and with a deep sigh and an unsubtle eye roll, he recites, “Jimin thinks—” Jimin makes a noise of objection. “We think,” Seokjin amends, “that you might benefit from some structured social events—”

“Not interested.”

“Just listen,” Jimin insists.

“As you may know, we have a product launch in a couple weeks—” Jimin waves his fists in a tiny cheer and then takes Seokjin’s cutlery out of his hands and resumes eating Seokjin’s steak. “And there’s a gala—”

“Absolutely not interested.”

“And my business associate who is, by the way, a rising star in the company—”

“Brilliant,” Jimin adds around a mouthful.

“And who happens to be single—”

“Gorgeous.” Jimin does something with his tongue that doesn’t seem to have anything to do with the steak.

“No. Nope. No.”

“You’d be doing her a big favor.”

“Sorry, no.”

“Namjoon, seriously.” Jimin points the steak knife at him. “You can’t just—”

“I’m seeing someone.”

Jimin lowers his utensils in dramatic slow motion. And waits. Namjoon turns to Seokjin, hoping for an assist, but his eyebrows are hiked up and he seems as content as Jimin to stare Namjoon down until he cracks.

“I don’t really want to talk about it.” Jimin and Seokjin look at each other and something happens with Jimin’s eyebrows that gives Namjoon a deep feeling of foreboding. “It’s new. Ish. Fairly new. Recent.”

With terrifying placidity, Jimin leans toward Seokjin and slices a chunk off his steak. “Where did you two meet?” He cuts the chunk of steak in half, his eyes on Namjoon.

“Um. We met. Online.” Jimin’s eyebrows do the scary jump again and he continues his knifework, the steak starting to resemble something that might be fed to small children or rodents. “Lots of people meet online. There’s nothing wrong with it.”

“Nothing wrong with it,” Seokjin agrees, and then clamps his lips together at Jimin’s slow intake of breath.

“Well we’d love to meet her. Wouldn’t we, Seokjin?”

“She’s traveling at the moment.” Jimin makes the smallest movement that can legitimately be classified as a smile. He thinks Namjoon is lying. He thinks he made her up. And, well, she isn’t made up. Not exactly. She exists, in a sense. And they are seeing each other, in a manner of speaking. “To Busan, actually. I might go with her.”

“Really.”

“Yes. If I can, you know, schedule. Hopefully. I was invited.”

“Were you.” He spears a particle of steak and deposits it in his mouth. “And what’s her name?”

“Jungsoon.”

👸🏻

💬  6:47 AMChongji ⚔Good tidings, agissi!2 more messages

Jungkook stares at the message preview. Good tidings? What exactly are tidings? After deciding last night that he’d give this Chongji person a chance, he deliberately did not check his account again, figuring he could come back with more energy and a positive outlook after a good night’s sleep. But even the preview makes him feel tired and out of his depth.

Before he can do anything about the waiting messages, there’s a distant slam and rapid-fire shouted instructions that he can’t catch but doesn’t actually need to hear because he and Hoseok have a routine for these visits. Jungsoon’s royal guard will have to wait.

“What is this?” Hoseok wants to know when Jungkook takes him into the first pink-lit growing room.

“I thought I’d switch things up a little. There’s only so many times I can listen to ‘Moonlight Sonata’ in one day. It isn’t good for my state of mind, and I don’t think the plants are crazy about it either, to be honest. They’re really into Lee Sun-hee, though. Check it out.” He strokes the bright green leaves of a deulkkae.

Hoseok purses his lips and continues down the aisle between the walls of plants growing from styrofoam forms. He turns around at the end of the row. “Love ballads, huh?”

“They like it.”

“I don’t know, aren’t love ballads kinda sappy? Try them on something grittier. Give them some Drake. Give them some Lil Pump.”

Jungkook frowns and gives the deulkkae a consoling pat. “I’ve been having trouble with one of the light arrays. Come see.”

And that’s how the whole day goes. Hoseok can’t figure out the problem with the lights, so he calls an electrician. Jungkook reluctantly reprograms the playlists to incorporate some of Hoseok’s choices, figuring it isn’t worth the argument because he’ll change it back as soon as Hoseok’s gone. They make a calendar for harvesting the sesame leaves and then the strawberries.

It isn’t until evening, when Hoseok would normally be saying goodbye until his next inspection in a few weeks, that he drops the biggest news.

“So I hate to spring this on you, but I’m actually going to hang here a few days. I can make up a bed in the office, though, so you don’t have to worry about me being in your hair.”

“Don’t be ridiculous, hyung. There’s plenty of room here. You can have my bed and I’ll take the couch—”

“No, no, stop it. I’ll take the couch. Or I’m fine in the office, really. I don’t want to be in your way.”

“You’re not in my way. It’ll be nice to have company.”

Hoseok pushes out his lips and croons in his saddest baby voice, “Is our Jungkookie getting lonely here all by himself?”

“Maybe a little.”

Hoseok wraps his hands around Jungkook’s throat and throttles him affectionately until Jungkook laughs, gently extricates himself, and goes to find extra bedlinens.

Most days he doesn’t mind being here alone, taking care of the plants, logging their progress, checking to make sure the equipment is in good working order. The work is straightforward, easy but rewarding, seeing his plants grow, harvesting them when the time comes, planting and tending a new crop. It leaves him plenty of time for his hobbies, working out and gaming, listening to music and doing some sketches when he feels like it. Most of the time he feels thankful to have lucked into a job he’s so well suited for, and most of the time he doesn’t mind at all that he spends so much time alone.

But Hoseok’s right that lately he’s been getting lonely. Feeling kind of stir crazy. It isn’t like he has to be on the premises around the clock, every day—most of the essential functions of the grow rooms are automated and he just has to make sure everything is working as it should. He’s more of a caretaker than a farmer. But the farm is kind of in the middle of nowhere. There isn’t much to do for entertainment around here, and he doesn’t have any friends nearby, so he spends pretty much all his time alone with the plants except for Hoseok’s check-ins every couple weeks. It’s what spurred him to look into the roleplay thing in the first place. It seemed like the best of all possible worlds: he could interact with other people, sort of, without having to travel to where they are, and it would relieve the monotony of his routine without requiring the same kind of commitment a real-life friendship would demand. If it works out. He wants it to work out.

He lets Hoseok occupy his attention until he dozes off midway through watching Jungkook play Overwatch. He tucks a blanket around him and tiptoes to his bedroom, and then it’s just him and his laptop and the waiting messages.

It’s after midnight, so maybe Chongji has gone to sleep and he can see what he’s written without the pressure of having to pick up a conversation. He taps his trackpad and the thread opens to two messages dated last night, several hours after their chat, plus the one he saw this morning, now a good 18 hours old. Does this guy sleep at all?

Chongji waits at the meeting place they arranged, just within the cover of the dense woods blanketing the mountainside. He’s nervous. Although this is a task he was trained for, born for even, the risk to himself and his charge is considerable, and the weight of his duty lies heavy on his shoulders.

He doesn’t know what to expect of this princess. Her upbringing might make her delicate and unsuited to the discomforts of travel. They have no choice but to undertake the first leg of the journey on foot. He has a relative a day’s walk into the countryside, and there they can borrow horses. He doesn’t dare try to find mounts any closer to the palace for fear they’ll be noticed. If the princess isn’t up to the exertion of a hard day’s hike through the mountains— Well, he’ll figure out a way.

The afternoon has faded to twilight before he’s alerted to the sounds of her approach: the crunch of dried leaves underfoot, a rustling in the underbrush, the snap of a twig. And then he catches sight of her.

He did have an expectation, he realizes now. Somehow in his mind’s eye, he saw her in hwarot like in her profile picture: her hands concealed in wide sleeves, hair elaborately coiled and pinned, full skirts heavy with embroidery. Instead, the person who emerges in front of him is dressed simply—disguised in a shapeless magoja and baji of drab dark gray that look like she stole them from the laundry of a stableboy. Her hair is braided, but it’s untidy and has partly come loose during her passage through the woods, with strands hanging free around her face.

Her color is high from the exertion of her walk, though she doesn’t seem to be in any distress—on the contrary, she seems invigorated. When their eyes meet, she smiles and bows, and it takes him longer than it should to respond with a deep bow of his own.

“Agissi, I’m relieved you arrived safely. Shall we depart, or do you need to rest?”

She looks surprised that he would even ask. “We should continue. I haven’t come far.”

That isn’t true. She’s come all the way from the palace, a long walk, and uphill. That she doesn’t require rest at this stage can only bode well for their progress overnight. It will be difficult and tiring, and though he knows the route well, the darkness will slow them, as will the need to avoid detection. It’s unlikely they’ll encounter anyone else if they keep to the edge of the woods and avoid roads, but they’ll still need to exercise caution.

He leads the way, turning back often to check that Jungsoon is still following, not falling behind or showing signs of struggling. On the contrary, she easily matches his pace and they make faster progress than he expected. She doesn’t hesitate at the river crossing, though it’s far more treacherous at night and in the rickety craft of a drunken boatman who surely will spend the small handful of coin Chongji slips him on enough spirits to make him forget their faces.

Even as the branches overhead begin to come alive with the first questioning chirps of the new day, Jungsoon stays close at his heels, uncomplaining.

“Let us stop here and take rest and sustenance, agissi,” he says at first light. Their night of walking has carried them over a series of foothills, and they’ve reached another stream, likely one of the many tributaries of the great river, carved through a shallow valley.

He lowers his pack and offers her a metal bowl to dip water from the stream. She drinks and hands it back to him, and he refreshes himself while she rolls up the sleeves of her magoja to wash her hands in the icy water.

“I regret that I have nothing to offer but plain rice.”

It isn’t easy for Namjoon to put himself back in the roleplay. Jungsoon’s challenge has shaken him. Was it wrong to expect a princess to allow him to serve her? Did he inadvertently insult her by wanting to save her the indignity of tromping through the woods in search of food? He was only trying to play his part, but now he’s feeling unsure of himself. Her reaction felt combative. She’s so strong. He wasn’t expecting her to be this independent.

He doesn’t dislike it, exactly. In some ways this is better than what he imagined. He’d rather have a capable princess who speaks her mind than someone helpless and fragile, but he didn’t expect to feel so judged. He didn’t expect to worry that he might make a misstep just by trying to be helpful.

Jungsoon shoves her disorderly hair off her face and strides across the grassy riverbank and into the woods. Chongji gets to work making the fire and setting the rice to cook, and by the time the princess returns holding up the hem of her magoja to make a sack brimming with leaves and stems, the sun is up and the rice is almost to the boil. She crouches at the water’s edge to pick the edible parts out of her harvest and tosses the tough stems into the water to be carried away by the current.

Chongji steps back when she approaches the cooking rice and drops in handfuls of leaves, tears mushrooms into chunks and tosses them in and then crouches to stir the bubbling porridge. He has to admit, it looks better than plain rice. Smells better, too, and when Jungsoon grants him permission with a nod and he’s finally allowed a steaming spoonful, there’s no question she’s made the most palatable travel rations he can remember eating.

She watches him, chewing on a leaf from a handful she’s kept in reserve, and smiles when he reaches eagerly for another spoonful. “Better than getting a rash from eating toxic plants, isn’t it? Or trying to finish our journey with the runs.” She tips her head to the sky and laughs, and Chongji concentrates on the food and tries to ignore the heat climbing up his neck.

“We should rest,” Chongji says when they’ve finished eating and he’s cleaned and packed away the pot. “We made good progress last night, but there
